newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai economic minister a veteran economist.
newsitem.headline: New Thai economic minister a veteran economist.

text.p: Thailand's new deputy prime minister in charge of the economy, Virabongsa Ramangkura, is a former finance minister, a veteran economist -- and, at least until now, a vocal critic of the present government.

Virabongsa, 54, played a key role in managing economic turmoil in the 1980s. He presided over the devaluation of the baht in 1984 and direct assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in the early 1980s.
He served as a finance minister in 1990 and deputy finance minister in 1992.

Virabongsa, known among locals as "Dr Krong (Thin and Tall)", had served as adviser to powerful Prime Minister Prem Tinsulanonda who was a premier for most of the 1980s when the foundation of a decade-long boom was laid.
Prem is now a respected statesman and a privy councillor who is said to be close to the revered King Bhumibol Adulyadej.

After receiving a doctorate degree in Economics from the University of Pennsylvania, he started a teaching career at Thailand's prestigious Chulalongkorn University where he was dean of the Faculty of Economics between 1981-1983.
He also briefly served as an adviser to Laos' economic and planning ministry during the early 1990s.
Virabongsa was known to be a staunch critic of the current government before being nominated for the post.
He had urged Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to accept the bitter pills prescribed by the IMF to save Thailand's messy economy and to restore the confidence of foreign investors.

"While there is still confidence in Thailand, there is a severe lack of confidence -- internally and externally -- in the management acumen of the Thai government," he recently told an economic seminar.
"Sentiment can hold as long as the government acts without flinching. Any attempt to fudge things now will be a disaster," he said.
Between 1982-1986, Thailand drew around $750 million each year from IMF loans, finance ministry officials said.
The debts were fully repaid by 1991, when Thailand liberalised its financial sector by accepting obligations under Article 8 of the IMF.

The minister, who is a member of Bank of Thailand's board of directors, is also known to be very critical of the management of the central bank. He recently suggested that "major surgery" was needed to restructure the organisation.
The central bank revealed earlier this month that it spent around 430 billion baht supporting ailing finance companies.
The financial malaise forced the authorities to suspend the operation of 42 cash-strapped finance firms on the top of 16 already suspended late June.
